before.label: Lamp
before.description: A movable source of light, not a physical ray.

after.label: Two lamps H/L + movable cover
after.description: Two lamps can shine at the same time. Their fixed marks are H and L on the positions card. A separate opaque cover can screen either lamp before its light reaches the opening; it does not cover the opening or a patch on the receiving screen. The comparison record supplies the trial observations: this game is not a live light simulation.

before.label: Two lamp positions
before.description: Two marked source positions permit a deliberate comparison without changing the aperture.

after.label: H above O; L below O; screen beyond O
after.description: Side view of the authored setup: both lamps are left of the small aperture O; a white receiving screen is on the right, in the dark room. H is one unit above O, L one unit below. The lamps are equally far left of O, and the screen is that same horizontal distance to its right. Units are arbitrary. Keep both lamps, O and the screen fixed; change only which lamp is covered. Light travels through uniform air, and the two receiving patches can be distinguished.

before.label: Camera obscura
before.description: In darkness an inverted image appears: upper and lower paths cross at the aperture. This demonstration is not an exclusive-inventor claim.

after.label: Camera obscura: doorway top appears below
after.description: The dark-room camera forms an inverted courtyard image: the upper doorway appears below and the lower paving above. The same opening and receiving screen can then be used with the two fixed lamps. This is a familiar construction, not an exclusive-inventor claim.

before.label: Ray diagram
before.description: Straight lines model light propagation in a uniform medium; a ray is a representation, not a luminous thread.

after.label: Equal steps: H → lower; L → upper
after.description: Use the corrected proof’s discipline: preserve equal relations rather than trust a sketch. Assume a straight light path in uniform air. Along one straight line, equal horizontal runs have equal vertical changes. H→O drops one unit; the equally long run beyond O drops one more, reaching the lower screen mark (−1). L→O rises one unit; continuing equally far rises one more, reaching the upper mark (+1). Thus H→lower and L→upper. The earlier equality reasoning helps work out this consequence; the old triangle proof does not establish the physical straight-path assumption. A ray is a drawn path, not a luminous thread.

before.label: Crossed rays
before.description: Tracing paths through the opening explains the image inversion geometrically.

after.label: Crossing paths invert the courtyard image
after.description: The straight path from the doorway’s top crosses the aperture and reaches the lower part of the screen; the path from the paving reaches the upper part. This agrees with the inverted camera image. In the marked lamp setup the same geometry gives H→lower and L→upper. Paths cross at O, but a crossing drawn on paper alone does not show whether the light contributions remain separable. Covering just one lamp can test that claim.

before.label: Predicted spots
before.description: The diagram predicts where light from each marked position should reach the screen.

after.label: Cover H → lower patch should vanish
after.description: Prediction before consulting the trial: both lamps uncovered should give two patches, H at the lower mark and L at the upper. If each contribution continues independently through O, covering H should remove only the lower patch and leave the upper one. Uncover H: both return. Cover L instead: only the upper patch should vanish, leaving the lower one. The geometry tells us which patch belongs to which lamp; selective removal tests whether crossing makes their contributions inseparable.

before.label: Comparison record
before.description: The lamp is moved between the specified positions and the observed spots are recorded. This is a deliberate test of this arrangement.

after.label: H covered: lower gone; L covered: upper gone
after.description:
Supplied observations for the authored trial, with lamps, aperture and receiving screen fixed:
Both uncovered: upper and lower patches present.
H covered: lower patch absent; upper remains.
H uncovered again: both present.
L covered: upper patch absent; lower remains.
L uncovered again: both present.
Each disappearance matches the prediction. The record changes one cover condition at a time and includes restoration; it is not a claim that merely moving one lamp tested two simultaneous light contributions.

before.label: Optical model
before.description: The same ray geometry accounts for the image and the moved-source observations. It does not settle all questions of vision.

after.label: Crossing preserves H/lower and L/upper
after.description: Geometry predicted H→lower and L→upper; the supplied trial removed just the corresponding patch whenever H or L was screened, and restored it when uncovered. Therefore, in this aperture arrangement crossing did not destroy source-to-patch correspondence. This counts against an inseparable-mixture account in which separate contributions could not emerge after meeting at O. The same straight-path representation explains the courtyard image’s inversion. Keep the distinction between a represented path, the supplied observation, and the supported conclusion; this is not a proof of every claim about light or sight.

before.label: Optical question
before.description: Light reaching an eye still needs an account of image formation and perception. A successful aperture demonstration is not the entire theory of sight.

after.label: Light path explained; eye sensing still open
after.description: The earlier dark-Moon case showed why an observation can support a prediction without selecting a unique complete account. Here the selective-cover test supports separate light paths through the opening; it can reject the stated inseparable-mixture consequence. But a receiving screen does not sense. This trial does not decide how an eye senses light, what structures do the sensing, or how perception occurs: rival eye accounts could agree on every patch in this record. Do not turn success on light propagation into a complete theory of vision.
